Summary
An AWS account is a resource container that facilitates your ability to access AWS services and
provision resources to host your applications and data. The architecture of an AWS account
ensures that the resources you create within the account are visible to only those who have
access to the account. This enforces stringent security, ensuring one customer cannot access
the resources of another without appropriate permissions.

85 AWS Accounts, Multi-Account Strategies, and AWS Organizations
Customers can create numerous AWS accounts for different workloads and application stacks
– they can also adopt strategies to separate environments of an individual application lifecycle
by creating a separate account for each environment of the applications, such as one account
for development, one for testing, and another for production. This ability to host different
applications and environments of an application across different accounts ensures isolation
and separation. Also, it reduces the blast radius of any disasters occurring in one account,
preventing them from affecting resources in another. Businesses will also need to consider
separating accounts from a compliance and governance perspective. For example, you would
not want your customer-facing applications to necessarily reside in the same AWS accounts as
your internal operations workloads.
As part of preparing for the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner exam, understanding this basic
concept is vital. Many businesses will have thousands of accounts, so naturally, you must also
be able to manage multiple accounts efficiently. This chapter introduced you to the features of
the AWS Organization service and core offerings, which are vital to ensuring reliable, cost-
effective, and secure management of an organization's multi-account architecture. The
importance of clubbing related accounts using OUs can help with efficient management. Using
service control policies (SCPs), you learned how to restrict what services, resources, and
actions can be taken in AWS member accounts. Furthermore, you also learned about the
benefits of consolidated billing, which can help customers reduce overall costs resulting from
volume discounts. In addition, the ability to share resources between member accounts can
also further optimize your total spending in the cloud.
From a practical perspective, you learned how Belly Brew Co. Limited would use the AWS
Organization service to separate the different environments of the customer-facing web
application. In addition, the company would require accounts for foundational services and
other internal business processes. SCPs will be crafted to ensure only approved services and
resources can be created in those accounts. You would not want to give unrestricted access to
spin up any resources in your corporate accounts, which could have cost implications as well as
security issues.
In this chapter, you learned how AWS accounts, multi-account strategies, AWS Organizations,
and AWS Control Tower help structure and govern cloud environments. In the next chapter, we
will focus on securing access within those environments by using AWS Identity and Access
Management, IAM users, groups, policies, roles, AWS Identity Center, Amazon Cognito, and

Chapter 4 88
5
AWS Access Management
Now that you have created your first AWS account, you must ensure that access to the account
is secured and that only authorized individuals in your organization can consume services and
provision required resources for your approved projects and workloads.
AWS offers several services to ensure you grant access to only authorized individuals and use
the principle of least privilege (POLP) when idx_a6316d4d assigning permissions and rights to those
individuals. Furthermore, applications you deploy on AWS may require access to specific AWS
services. For example, an application may need access to an Amazon S3 bucket to upload log
files or a database to query customer records. Using AWS's suite of access management tools,
you can ensure that those applications are granted only the necessary permissions for those
services and resources to function correctly.
This chapter will teach you about the AWS Identity and Access Management service, a core
component offering authentication idx_53d9b673 and authorization services for your AWS account and the
workloads you deploy. In addition, you will also learn about other authentication and
authorization services and technologies that cater to a wide range of use cases — from
implementing and managing federated access and single sign-on capabilities for your
workforce to building a sign-up and sign-in solution for your applications.
This chapter discusses the importance of building access solutions according to the principle of
least privilege, protecting the root user account, and using the appropriate tools based on the
use case. This chapter will also showcase methods used to access the AWS account and how
permissions are granted through policy documents.
The following topics are covered in this chapter:
Managing access with AWS Identity and Access Management
Centralizing workforce access with AWS Identity Center
•
•
Managing application-user identities with Amazon Cognito
Integrating Microsoft directory services with AWS Directory Service
Managing access with AWS Identity and Access
Management
AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) is a core idx_bf572c71 security service that enables you
to securely control access to your AWS account. AWS IAM offers two idx_c20ed59e key services:
authentication and authorization. Authentication enables the identification and verification
of a trusted identity, which can be an IAM user idx_5a7d2903 or an IAM role (discussed in the IAM users and
IAM roles sections later in this chapter). This trusted identity authenticates against your AWS
account by presenting a set of credentials that AWS IAM will verify and, if correct, grant access
to the AWS account.
Now, although access to the AWS account has been granted through the authentication

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 4 88
chunks.content:
process, the identity still cannot perform any action in the account until you authorize it with
specific permissions. Here, the identity is also idx_f9f35e88 known as a principal, which is any entity, such
as human users, applications, or services, that can access a particular resource. Principals can
be granted permissions via policies to access specific services and perform certain actions
against those services.
With both authentication and authorization, you can decide who or what can access your AWS
account, which services can be consumed, and what actions can be performed against the
resources in your account.
For example, you can create a set of credentials for the principal (also an identity) 'Alice' to
access your AWS account. Alice can then use these credentials to authenticate against your
AWS account. Next, you can define idx_bc6c3a19 policies (also known as permissions) so that Alice is
authorized to access Amazon S3, which is an object idx_9d8c8b49 storage solution, and download data from
a specific S3 bucket. Similarly, you can authorize another principal, such as an application
running on an EC2 instance (which is a virtual server), with the permission to update a
database with customer orders.
Authorization requests can be made by principals in your AWS account or from other trusted
AWS accounts.
Before examining the different types of principals you can define permissions for, it's
important to appreciate the role of the root user, which represents the owner of your AWS
account. The next section delves into this further.
•
•

chunks.heading: Chapter 5 90
chunks.content:
Chapter 5 90
The role of the root user account
The root user is the owner of the AWS account. It is represented by the email address and
password you chose when setting up the idx_b81346b1 AWS account. This root user is the absolute 'God' of
your account, meaning that it has full unrestricted access to the services in the idx_088bcdeb account and can
launch any type of resources within the confines of the limits and quotas imposed by AWS. The
only exception to this is that if the AWS account is a member of an AWS Organization, then you
can use Service Control Policies (SCPs) to restrict idx_2a44beb3 specific access and permissions for the root
user.
The root user can also perform certain actions that no other IAM user can. These include:
Change your account settings.
Close your AWS account. Only the root user can close the account.
Amazon Simple Storage Services (Amazon S3). Certain actions on the Amazon S3
service, such as enabling multi-factor idx_89e6dd55 authentication for an Amazon S3 bucket
Sign up for a US Gov idx_97afa1fc Cloud account. This requires additional prerequisites.
Viewing certain tax invoices.
Restore IAM permissions—for any administrator user, if no other user has
administrative access.
Activate IAM access to Billing and Cost management – by default, only the root user
can access this service. However, AWS strongly recommends that you do not use the
root user account for day-to-day operations. Activating this feature enables you to
grant permissions to other IAM users to access billing and cost information. An
example use case for this is granting access to members of the Finance department.
AWS also recommends that you idx_41c0f859 enhance the login security of the root user account by enabling
multi-factor authentication. This ensures that a bad actor cannot easily gain access to your
AWS account if they happen to know your email address and password. This feature is
discussed in the next section.
The root user and multi-factor authentication
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is the practice of using an idx_d44573a3 additional authentication
factor in addition to your standard idx_811dff82 username and password. MFA follows a principle of
authenticating idx_cb81d24f based on a minimum of two of the following factors:
What you know: This is a standard authentication factor that requires the trusted
identity to present a set of credentials (for example, username and password) to verify
their identity. It's based on the idea that only the identity will have access to these
credentials.
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
91 AWS Access Management
What you have: This is an additional authentication factor that requires the trusted
identity to possess some device (physical or virtual, like an app) that can be used to
generate a one-time password (or PIN). This can also be a mobile number that would

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 5 90
chunks.content:
receive a text SMS with the PIN. It's based on the idea that only the identity would
possess this device (or a specific mobile number).
What you are: This is an additional authentication factor that requires the identity to
verify their physical being, such as a fingerprint, retina scan, etc.
MFA thus refers to answering multiple idx_251f2870 challenges to verify your identity, such as what you know
and what you have in the authentication process. AWS customers can also configure their
accounts with a what you are type MFA by using a biometrics-enabled authenticator.
Using MFA drastically reduces the chances idx_21bcd049 of a malicious attacker impersonating you. If the
attacker has access to your credentials, hopefully, they will not have access to your physical or
virtual device that generates those one-time PINs.
AWS enables its customers to idx_ece29a1a configure MFA both for the root user as well as for IAM users,
and most companies will implement MFA as a standard security protocol along with ensuring
the use of password complexity to make brute force attacks difficult.
When you have hundreds or even thousands of users who need an IAM user ID to access your
AWS account, ensuring that everyone chooses a complex password can be an administrative
overhead. Luckily, AWS offers a feature to enforce this, and the next section covers this in more
detail.
Enforcing password complexity
Password complexity refers to idx_abc41f00 the ability to construct a password that is hard to guess. This
involves combining letters, numbers, and symbols while containing a minimum set of
characters. The password must not be made of dictionary words, and depending on the
identity and management service, its security can be enhanced using passphrases.
AWS offers a feature that allows you to enforce rules on how passwords should be defined
using the password policy feature located in the Account Settings section of the IAM
dashboard, as depicted in Figure 5.1:
•
•

Chapter 5 92
Figure 5.1: Password policy settings
As a company, you can define idx_1795905e password complexity rules that apply to all IAM user accounts
created in the AWS account. This makes it easier to fulfill compliance requirements.
In the next section, you will learn more about IAM users. These are identities that usually
represent your human workforce and need access to your AWS account to design, build, and
manage your products and services.
IAM users
An IAM user is an identity you create for a idx_b112e58d trusted human user to be able to authenticate
against your AWS account. This IAM user can idx_61616b71 represent a development team member, server
administrator, or the company's CEO. The trusted individual uses the IAM user's credentials to
log into the AWS account and perform any tasks permitted based on permissions you assign
using IAM policies (discussed later in this chapter).
IAM user credentials can also be idx_34bea248 used by non-human users, such as an application running on
an EC2 instance that needs access to other services on AWS. However, this access method is
not recommended, as managing credentials for non-human principals can be an
administrative overhead. Furthermore, using IAM user credentials embedded in application
code carries a much higher risk since the idx_dd686e51 credentials are usually stored in plain text and could
fall into the wrong hands. Instead, AWS recommends you use IAM roles for this use case, which
will be discussed shortly.
93 AWS Access Management
When accessing your AWS account, IAM users must perform a login exercise and verify their
identities using the credentials defined for their IAM user account. Depending on the method
of access, AWS offers multiple credential types as follows:
Username and Password: These credentials allow you to access your AWS
Management Console. To sign in, you must provide the AWS account ID or the
account alias in addition to the username and password. AWS lets you create a URL to
customize your AWS Account ID (where you can substitute the ID for an alias). This
URL is formatted as https://My_AWS_Account_ID.signin.aws.amazon.com/console/
Access Keys: These comprise an access key ID (for example, AKIAIOSFOFFD7EXAMPLE)
and a secret access key (for example, wJalrXUvdFEMI/K4FDENG/bKxRflCYEXAMPLEKEY).
Access keys are used to access your AWS account programmatically idx_a79cc63c using the
command-line interface (CLI). This access method requires you to install the CLI
tools on your local machine, which you can download from https://aws.amazon.com/
cli/, and interact with AWS using commands and API calls. You can have a maximum
of two access keys for each IAM user.
X.509 Certificates: This method has been deprecated for most services. However, IAM
users can still use X.509 certificates to authenticate for some AWS services like AWS

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 5 92
chunks.content:
IoT.
Often, different teams within a company idx_efdc544c share common job functions. While each team
member will require an IAM user account, managing permissions becomes much easier when
you group users into IAM groups and assign permissions at the group level. The next section
discusses IAM groups in idx_860bebb6 detail.
IAM groups
IAM groups allow you to manage user idx_efb82fa9 permissions more efficiently. Permissions are assigned
to groups, and users who belong to those groups automatically inherit those permissions. For
example, the development team idx_4cfa7eae might need access to a set of DevOps tools, while the
infrastructure engineering team may require access to networking and compute services.
Rather than assigning permissions to each IAM user individually, you can place users into
groups and assign the necessary permissions to the group. Users in the group will inherit the
group's permissions, as shown in Figure 5.2:
•
•
•

chunks.heading: Chapter 5 94
chunks.content:
Chapter 5 94
Figure 5.2: Using IAM groups to manage permission assignment
As per the diagram in Figure 5.2, assigning permissions to groups is easier than assigning these
permissions directly to each user, as it idx_fc461067 involves fewer permissions and policy documents to
manage. In this example, you only need to assign two sets of permissions to two groups. Users
within the groups will inherit the idx_e55dd5b9 permissions applied at the group level. This also reduces the
management overhead when team members change roles or join and leave the company.
The next section will teach how permissions are assigned to IAM users and groups.
IAM policies
Permissions are assigned using IAM policy idx_d3ed8bc2 documents. There are two types of policies you can
configure on AWS – IAM Policies and idx_973705f9 resource-based policies. IAM policies idx_674ef241 are known as
identity-based policies, and they are directly assigned to identities such as IAM users, IAM
roles (discussed in the IAM roles section), or groups of IAM users who need idx_bf9fcacc access to services
and resources in your AWS account. IAM policy documents are idx_9f4ceecb written in JavaScript Object
Notation (JSON) format.
95 AWS Access Management
With IAM policies, you can define permissions idx_eaf94f2e that cover specific granular actions that can be
performed against resources. This allows you to apply the POLP, ensuring that the identity
does not have more permissions than necessary for their job role.
For example, some users may be permitted to launch and configure EC2 instances, but only a
few senior users should be allowed to terminate any EC2 instances.
IAM policies can be applied to IAM identities such as IAM users, IAM roles, and groups of users
within the same account in which they were created.
There are three types of identity-based policies:
Managed AWS policies: These are idx_1b2da861 standard, pre-defined policy documents written in
JSON and managed solely by AWS. These boilerplate policies can be used to
standardize permissions for your identities. The policies are created independently of
any identity and can be assigned to one or more identities in your AWS account. You
cannot edit these policies.
Customer-managed policies: These idx_599c40e1 are policies you create and manage and assign to
IAM Identities. Unlike many AWS managed policies, you can define more granular
permissions against specific resources in your AWS account. You can have up to five
versions of a customer-managed policy, allowing you to revert to previous versions if
required.
Inline policies: These policies are idx_d7e39548 created for a specific identity, such as an IAM user.
They are not independent of that identity and cannot be attached to other identities.
This ensures a strict one-to-one relationship between an identity and a policy. AWS

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 5 94
chunks.content:
recommends using idx_7baec964 inline policies sparingly because they require more administrative
effort than managed policies. They idx_e4fc782a also make tracking what policies you have
configured in your AWS account more difficult.

signifies that they are managed by AWS.

"s3:GetObject"
],

This policy grants the identity it is attached to the ability to read and download objects from
the bellybrew ‑ source ‑ code S3 bucket.
Because this is an IAM policy, you do not need to specify the identity. Instead, you can attach
the policy to the identity that needs idx_007fc6d6 the permissions specified in the policy. The idx_07df61b4 following
represents the anatomy of a typical IAM policy:
Version: This is the currently supported version of the JSON document, which, at the
time of writing this book, is 2012-10-17.
Statement: This is the beginning of the policy statement. Under the statement block,
you can have multiple permissions blocks, enabling you to apply various permissions
across different AWS services and resources. The preceding code snippet shows only
one statement block.
Sid: The Sid (Statement ID) is an optional identifier that gives a unique name or label
to individual statements idx_7f682ddd within a policy. It can help distinguish between different
statements, mainly when a policy contains multiple statements.
Effect: This defines whether the statement block is going to allow some action or deny
it. In this example, the Effect is set to Allow.
Action: This is the specific permission you grant or deny to the identity to perform. The
Action statement defines the AWS service and one or more actions that are permitted
against resources of the Service. In this example, the service is Amazon S3, and the
action permitted is GetObject, which would allow the identity to read/download the
object from the bucket.
The Get action, for example, includes several sub-operations, such as GetObject, that
allow you to read/download objects. Another sub-operation is GetBucketVersioning,
which enables you to retrieve a bucket's versioning state.
Resource: This policy idx_54fbe5fa component defines the actual resource against which the
identity is granted specific permission. In the previous code snippet, the ARN of the
Belly Brew Co. Limited idx_821e1b78 bucket is provided as arn:aws:s3:::bellybrew ‑ source ‑ code/

also known as a wildcard, states that the identity can access all contents of the
bellybrew ‑ source ‑ code bucket.
Likewise, if you set the ARN to a wildcard (asterisk) and do not define a specific bucket,
then the identity can perform the said action against all buckets in the AWS account. In

Condition: You can also define conditional statements in your policy so that the policy
is only applicable if the condition is met. An example might be to restrict identities
from creating new S3 buckets once the request comes from a source IP address that
represents your corporate network. This way, you add a layer of security to ensure that
requests come from authorized sources.
Sometimes, when you apply specifically complex policies to Identities, there may be issues
because those policies have not idx_3fabf05f been defined correctly. You can idx_2ea27748 use the IAM policy simulator to
help you troubleshoot your policies and identify potential access or permissions issues. This is
discussed in the next section.
IAM Policy Simulator
The IAM Policy Simulator is a tool for analyzing whether your IAM users, groups, or roles can
perform specific actions with their assigned idx_c2526745 permissions. This is particularly idx_a632642d useful when
troubleshooting complex permission sets and trying to identify the root cause of any missing
permissions.
In Figure 5.4, you will note the permissions defined for an IAM user called Bob. The user only
has a single policy attached, granting full access to the Amazon DynamoDB service. When
running tests to see if Bob can perform the GetObject action against the Amazon S3 service,
the results show Denied.
•
You can access idx_a869c7ed the simulator at https://policysim.aws.amazon.com/. You must log
in to your AWS account to use the service.
Note
99 AWS Access Management
Figure 5.4: IAM Policy Simulator
This is because Bob has not been granted permission to access Amazon S3. While this example
is simple, imagine troubleshooting more complex policies. The IAM Policy Simulator also lets
you test your new policies to ensure idx_a18c1cb5 they perform as expected. You can then test out idx_3cecd26c the policy
before deploying it on AWS.
In the next section, you will learn more about another IAM identity feature: IAM Roles.
IAM roles
An IAM Role is like an IAM user, except it is idx_13f77da8 created independently of any specific human user.
Whereas an IAM user account is usually made for a particular person, IAM roles are intended
to be assumed by one or more principals idx_56ef0b48 who need access to specific services and resources in
your AWS account.
Authorized principals can access a particular resource by assuming the role if the role has been
configured to trust that principal and it has permissions for the resource. This means that an
IAM role is configured with a trust policy that identifies the principal who can assume the role.

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 5 98
chunks.content:
Additionally, an IAM policy is attached to the role, defining the permissions the role grants to
the principal.
IAM roles only grant temporary credentials to principals who assume them. The AWS Security
Token Service (AWS STS) entirely manages these idx_c90d1e9b credentials. You do not create usernames
and passwords or access keys (long-term credentials) for IAM roles. Instead, the AWS STS
service assigns temporary credentials to the principal who assumes the role. These temporary
credentials will include an access key ID, a secrets access key, and a security token. The security
token expires after a short period, and the AWS STS service renews the credentials before
expiry if the principal is still permitted access. This all happens transparently to the end user.
IAM roles are used in various scenarios, some of which will be covered in the following
subsections.

Chapter 5 100
Cross-account access
In Chapter 4, you learned about the idx_0d5f9ae9 importance of a multi-account idx_c000488d architecture. While having
multiple accounts offers more significant levels of security and isolation between your
workloads, how you configure access to those accounts is very important. The last thing you
want is for your workforce to have multiple IAM user accounts, one in each AWS account, to
grant them access to the various idx_bf624cd5 environments and applications you host.
Instead, you can configure cross-account access for your workforce using IAM roles. Using this
approach, you create all idx_e4b0c3f7 your IAM users within a single AWS account and grant them
permissions to assume IAM roles of other AWS accounts with the required level of access. So, in
the case of Belly Brew Co. Limited, you might create the IAM user accounts in idx_6bafa793 a separate AWS
account – you can call it the Identities AWS Account – and configure roles with relevant
permissions in the Development and Production accounts, allowing those IAM users the ability
to assume the roles. The permissions granted via those IAM roles would be based on their job
function and group membership within the Identities account.

the Development account without having to create a duplicate IAM user account for James in

If using the CLI or AWS API, the user idx_00bf36b4 must call the AssumeRole function to obtain
credentials for the s3updaterole role by specifying the idx_97887b2d role's ARN.
Another use case for IAM roles is granting users from external identity providers (outside the
AWS ecosystem) temporary credentials to access services and resources in your AWS accounts.
This is made possible by using identity idx_6934f4d8 federation, which idx_b48fc12b will be discussed in the next section.
IAM roles for identity federation
Identity federation is the process of granting access to identities authenticated by external,
trusted identity providers (IDPs) to services idx_04444bf9 and resources within your AWS account.
For example, Belly Brew Co. Limited has an idx_82c1056e on-premises IT environment that spans its head
offices and manufacturing plants across the UK. Employees at Belly Brew Co. Limited use the
on-premises identity provider, in this case Microsoft Active Directory, to authenticate against
on-premises workloads. Some of those users, such as developers and systems administrators,
now require access to resources in the AWS accounts. Rather than creating additional
credentials in the AWS accounts for those users (IAM user accounts), which would require the
users to remember multiple usernames and passwords, you can use identity federation to
authenticate those users against your AWS environment.You can then define IAM roles that
specify the permissions those users will have in your AWS accounts.
AWS Identity Federation supports SAML 2.0 (Security Assertion Markup Language 2.0),
allowing you to establish trust between your idx_1414802c organization, acting as the identity provider
(IdP), and AWS as the service idx_cd9416de provider. Using SAML, your users can access the AWS
Management Console through federated single sign-on (SSO) or gain federated access to
execute AWS API operations.
AWS Identity Federation also supports idx_b9e90087 web identity federation with OpenID Connect (OIDC)
providers such as Google and Facebook. This is usually used to provide authentication and
authorization for mobile and web-based applications. However, AWS recommends you use
Amazon Cognito for this scenario. This service has several additional features and security
tools, which will be discussed later in this chapter.
Another use case for IAM roles is the ability to grant temporary access to non-AWS workloads,
which will be idx_fb4bcc75 discussed next.
Note that when switching roles, you must know the destination AccountID
and the role name you need to assume.
Note
103 AWS Access Management
IAM roles anywhere
Previously, when you created IAM roles, they could only be assumed by identities in your AWS
account or other AWS accounts, as in the case with cross-account access discussed previously.

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 5 102
chunks.content:
However, IAM roles could only be idx_49236530 assumed by applications running on an AWS service, such as
an EC2 instance. An example scenario would be an application hosted on an EC2 instance that
requires access to an Amazon S3 bucket to upload log files.
But what about applications running on-premises or third-party cloud providers, which may
also require access to AWS services and resources? In this scenario, you would be embedding
long-term credentials, such as access keys, in your application code or using some
environmental variables to host these keys, but the security risk of this approach means that it
does not follow industry-standard best practice. This is because you are potentially storing
access keys in plain text within the application source code.
AWS now offers IAM Roles Anywhere, which addresses this issue – a service that allows you to
create a trust anchor to establish a trust relationship between the IAM Roles Anywhere service
and a Certificate Authority (CA) that issues idx_c1be998a X.509 certificates for your organization. The on-
premises server would present the certificate that the AWS IAM roles anywhere service
validates and maps the server to a specific IAM role. The on-premises server is then granted
permissions to access AWS services and resources as defined in the IAM policy attached to the
role.
To generate these X.509 certificates, you idx_616fb85c can either use a CA using AWS Private Certificate
Authority or a CA from idx_3321e9eb your public key infrastructure (PKI) provider.
Using IAM Roles Anywhere, you can authenticate non-AWS workloads using the trust anchor
and obtain temporary credentials from the IAM Role to access permitted AWS services and
resources.
So far, you have learned that IAM roles allow users and applications that run on resources such
as EC2 instances to access other AWS services and resources. But what about granting the
resources of one AWS service the ability to idx_7a30a3da access the resources of another AWS service? In the
next section, you will learn more about service roles that allow one AWS service to access
another service with specific permissions required for your application workflow.
AWS service roles
A service role allows an AWS service to perform actions against another service and its
resources on your behalf. Using a service role, you idx_3d498e50 can define a set of permissions the AWS
service needs to interact with other AWS services and resources in your account. You get to
decide the actions the service can take against another resource.

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 5 104
chunks.content:
Chapter 5 104
For example, a spreadsheet is stored in an Amazon S3 bucket (a storage platform). You need to
process the data in the spreadsheet and update a backend database table running on Amazon
DynamoDB (a NoSQL database solution). To help automate the process, you could use a
Lambda function (which offers serverless compute capabilities) and write code to extract the
data from the spreadsheet, process it, and then update the database.
The Lambda function will need permission to read the raw data from the S3 bucket and write
the processed data to the DynamoDB table. To facilitate this, you would create an appropriate
IAM role (with the necessary permissions) and associate it with the Lambda function. When
the function executes, it assumes this service role, allowing it to read data from the S3 bucket
and write to the DynamoDB table.
While creating identities and assigning appropriate levels of permissions following the
principle of least privilege is critical, monitoring the list of live and active identities in your
AWS account is equally important. Many organizations tend to have identities, such as IAM
user accounts, continue to exist long after they are required. This poses a security risk if
someone manages to guess the idx_8115ad49 username and password of an unused IAM user account or if
the access keys fall into the wrong hands. In the next section, you will learn about a tool you
can use to actively manage your IAM identities.
The AWS credentials report
You can download the AWS credentials idx_a98ee12b report to monitor idx_1a376975 a list of all IAM users you have
created in your AWS account. This comma-separated values (CSV) file, depicted in Figure 5.7,
is updated every four hours and enables idx_1dd82e72 you to audit your IAM user security posture.
Figure 5.7: AWS credentials report
Using this report, you can identify critical information about your IAM user accounts, such as
whether they have been configured with web console access, CLI access, set up with multi-
factor authentication, etc. You can also identify the last time the IAM user logged into the AWS
account, which can help identify stale and unused accounts.
In Figure 5.7, you will note that MFA has not been enabled for any IAM accounts. Furthermore,
even the root user account has yet to be configured with MFA, which poses an extremely high
risk to the account. A malicious attacker would need to guess the email address and the
password to gain full administrative rights to the account. AWS highly recommends you
configure MFA for the root user.
105 AWS Access Management
The AWS Credentials Report can give auditors a detailed breakdown of your IAM user and root
user configuration. It can also form part of your compliance reporting and documentation.
In the next section, you will learn idx_47da13ae about another identity and access management service

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 5 104
chunks.content:
specifically designed for managing your workforce identities across multiple AWS accounts in
your AWS Organization.
Centralizing workforce access with AWS Identity
Center
In the previous section, you learned idx_262ab668 how to design cross-account access for IAM user accounts
using IAM roles. This allows users in one AWS account to access services and resources in other
AWS accounts and prevents the creation of duplicate IAM user accounts in multiple AWS
accounts. Using IAM roles in this scenario to enable cross-account access offers several
benefits, including enforcing the principle of least privileged access and reducing the
management overhead associated with managing multiple (duplicate) IAM user accounts for
the same individual.
However, the cross-account idx_22e64433 design approach is cumbersome to set up. For every AWS account
the IAM user needs access to, you must create a specific IAM role with the necessary
permissions and trust policies. While creating IAM roles to allow users from other third-party
external accounts (such as business partners or service providers) is a viable option for this use
case, AWS offers an alternative solution for managing your workforce users' access to your
AWS Organization's member accounts. This alternative is the AWS Identity Center.
Previously dubbed the AWS Single Sign On (SSO) service, AWS Identity Center is explicitly
designed to manage your idx_e24f5779 organization's workforce idx_b4a8ae74 identities. The service offers a single space
from which you can create and assign groups of users and their permissions to AWS accounts
in your AWS Organizations. These permissions can be assigned based on job function or any
other security protocol your company follows. In addition, with its single sign-on capabilities,
the Identity Center makes it much easier to federate with external identity providers. It
seamlessly allows you to define access permissions through the various AWS accounts in your
organization.
Once configured, your workforce can access a single portal to authenticate against all your
AWS accounts (if the necessary group memberships and permission sets have been granted in
the Identity Center). A screenshot of a typical portal is depicted in Figure 5.8:

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 5 106
chunks.content:
Chapter 5 106
Figure 5.8: AWS Access Portal – IAM Identity Center
You must still use the AWS Identity and Access Management Service (AWS IAM) to manage
all your IAM roles. The Identity Center is designed to idx_c8027b95 manage your company's workforce
identities alone. The best part is you do not need to idx_629739d4 create and manage individual IAM roles or
worry about Account IDs and Role names when you try to access other AWS accounts in the
Organization.
In addition to granting your workforce access to your organization's various AWS member
accounts, the AWS Identity Center can also be configured to provide seamless access to
applications that those workforce users require, using idx_07308845 the same single sign-on (SSO)
capabilities. Applications such as Amazon Q Developer and Amazon Redshift offer integration
with the AWS Identity Center. Your workforce users can also be granted access to third-party
applications using SSO, such as Office 365, Salesforce, and many more.
In addition to managing identities for your workforce users, you must also decide how to
manage application end users. These users are not part of your technical workforce but are end
consumers of the applications you host on AWS. These users can be internal or external to the
organization, such as customers.
While IAM and AWS Identity Center are designed to help you configure authentication and
authorization for your organization's employees, you also need to consider how end users and
customers will authenticate with the idx_7c496f7f applications you host on AWS.
107 AWS Access Management
Customers only need to authenticate with the application itself, not with the underlying AWS
services or resources. This reflects a clear separation of roles: customers authenticate with the
application they use, while employees—such as developers and cloud engineers—
authenticate with the AWS platform to configure and manage the resources that host the
application.
The next section provides an overview of Amazon Cognito, a service designed to help you build
an identity platform for your application users.
Managing application-user identities with Amazon
Cognito
So far, you have learned how to create and manage identities that form part of your workforce.
These identities represent users idx_7f36790c who need access to your AWS accounts to design and build
solutions for your company. They also include users in idx_44fd8452 your business who need access to the
AWS accounts to manage security, auditing, and cost management.
In addition to these users, you need a mechanism to authenticate and authorize end users of
the web and mobile applications you host on AWS. These users can be considered customers of
your application, whether they are internal to the organization or external customers who

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 5 106
chunks.content:
purchase access to your products and services.
AWS offers Amazon Cognito, a service that idx_59835843 provides a customer identity and access
management (CIAM) service for your web and mobile applications. The service takes the
burden of building an identity and access management solution for your idx_380c1c27 applications by
offering a wide array of features that you can integrate with your application authentication
and authorization processes. These include a customizable user interface (UI) for sign-up and idx_d78b6c2f
sign-in web pages for your applications, enabling self-registration capabilities and multi-
factor authentication support.
With Amazon Cognito, you can create a user pool of identities (scalable to millions of users) or
integrate with social identity providers like OpenID (OIDC), such as Facebook, Google, and
Amazon. You can also integrate with idx_c7ac452c SAML 2.0-compatible providers, such as Microsoft Active
Directory.
There are two types of pools you can create with Amazon Cognito:
Amazon Cognito user pools: Offer authentication services to your application,
allowing it to host millions of users or federate with third-party identity providers,
such as Apple, Facebook, and idx_7f92ec9c Google. For federated access, the user pool manages
•

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 5 108
chunks.content:
Chapter 5 108
tokens issued by the identity provider. Amazon Cognito user pools also allow tracking
user devices, locations, and IP addresses.
Amazon Cognito identity pools: Allow authorization idx_3ef9e781 to access AWS services and
resources such as Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon S3, and Lambda serverless
components. Using IAM roles, you can enforce the principle of least privileged access to
AWS services. Amazon Cognito identity pools also enable you to define access for
unauthenticated (guest) users who may be permitted to access specific resources. This
can be useful when you build a web application that offers free vs. premium paid-for
services.
In addition to user identity management for internal workforce and application authentication
requirements, AWS also offers services to facilitate integration with Microsoft identity and
access management services, specifically Microsoft Active Directory. The next section provides
an overview of this offering.
Integrating Microsoft directory services with AWS
Directory Service
The Microsoft industry-recognized Active idx_76a0a4c7 Directory Service is a critical identity and access
management solution that underpins the very essence of identity management within the
Microsoft ecosystem.
Almost every Microsoft infrastructure idx_0aa16038 application and service requires an Active Directory
environment for user authentication and authorization, application management, and security
integration. Customers who wish to host Microsoft infrastructure applications on AWS often
require an Active Directory environment to be present. In the past, this would mean deploying
Active Directory on virtual machines accessible to those applications over appropriate network
connectivity.
AWS offers AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory (AWS Managed
Microsoft AD). This fully managed service reduces the idx_657a4fb9 administrative burden of hosting your
own AD servers in the cloud.
AWS Managed Microsoft AD offers the full spectrum of Active Directory services running as a
highly available pair of domain controllers across two availability zones connected to your
virtual private cloud (Amazon VPC). AWS idx_797b47e3 will manage the administration of the servers,
including software updates, backup, and data replication. With this deployment in place, you
can host Microsoft directory-aware applications, including Microsoft SharePoint, Exchange,
SQL Server-based applications, and more. The service also allows integration with Amazon
RDS for Microsoft SQL Server and the ability to configure trust relationships with on-premises
Active Directory environments for an authentic hybrid cloud experience.
•
109 AWS Access Management
In addition, you can join Amazon Workspace Windows desktops to the Active Directory
domain to enjoy benefits such as enhanced management idx_f05f5ed4 and security of your virtual desktops

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 5 108
chunks.content:
in the cloud. Amazon Workspaces is a fully managed idx_6f72767b end-user computing service that enables
you to deploy virtual Linux and idx_f03e300c Windows desktops in the cloud, accessible using thin client
machines or even web browser interfaces.
This section provided an overview of the AWS Directory Services for Microsoft Active Directory
and how to integrate Microsoft AD-aware applications within your AWS environments. In the
next section, you will have the opportunity to work in your AWS Development account, where
you will set up IAM users and groups. You will also idx_5be1a8a6 learn how to access the AWS account and
its services using the command line interface (AWS CLI).

Summary
AWS Identity and Access Management is a critical security service designed to ensure that only
authorized principals can access services and resources in your AWS account. The service also
enables you to configure strict password policies to enforce complexity and enhance login
security using multi-factor authentication. AWS recommends that both IAM and root user
accounts be configured with MFA.
It is paramount to understand the importance of applying the principle of least privileged
access, which reduces the risk of accidental configuration or recourse by unauthorized
personnel. In addition, limiting access to only authorized services and resources ensures that
the blast radius of any disasters caused by leaked credentials, which have come into the
possession of bad actors, is reduced.
In addition to enabling access to your workforce, you must design authorization for other
principals, such as services and applications that must interact with AWS resources. For
example, an application running on a web server may need access to a backend database. AWS
recommends that for such use cases, you must use IAM roles to grant temporary credentials
with only the necessary permissions required for the interaction. This prevents the need to
manage long-term credentials, such as access keys, which can pose a security risk and increase
119 AWS Access Management
administrative burden. IAM roles are also designed to enable entities external to the AWS
account to access services and resources through a trust policy, allowing you to design cross-
account access for third parties.
To manage your workforce identities, especially if you have an AWS Organization service to
manage multiple AWS accounts, use the Identity Center. You can create and manage workforce
identities with single sign-on capability. Rather than create duplicate identities in each AWS
account for the same individual, you can have a single Identity Center account that grants the
individual access to multiple AWS accounts in your organization.
Finally, you can build a customer identity management system (CISM) for your application
end users using AWS Cognito. The service enables you to integrate a sign-up and sign-in
feature into your applications, enabling your end users and customers to self-register for
access to your application. Amazon Cognito offers you the ability to create and manage a user

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 5 118
chunks.content:
pool within the service or integrate with third-party open identity providers such as Google
and Facebook for identity federation. Additionally, you can configure identity pools to grant
users direct access to resources running on services such as Amazon S3 and Amazon
DynamoDB. Amazon Cognito Identity Pools can also be used to grant unauthenticated or guest
access to certain resources. This can be particularly useful when you want to offer certain
services on trial or for free.
Ultimately, any reputable identity and access management service must ensure it offers
stringent authentication and authorization features that protect your cloud environment and
the applications you host within it. AWS offers a diverse set of services to fulfill a wide range of
customer requirements across its identity solutions.

6
Amazon Simple Storage Service
(Amazon S3)
Storage services are a significant component of cloud computing because almost every
application needs somewhere to host its data. Although cloud service providers like AWS have
offered cheap storage services due to economies of scale, you must evaluate your storage
requirements and design an appropriate storage lifecycle as an organization. Regulatory and
compliance requirements might require you to store data for as long as 7 to 10 years. However,
you must purge unwanted data from your storage systems to ensure effective cost
management and data security.
Storage services can host various data formats, from unstructured data such as documents,
emails, images, and video to structured formats such as lists and tables in a database. AWS
offers various storage options, each designed for specific data formats. This chapter introduces
storage concepts and then discusses a particular storage architecture: object storage with
Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).
Amazon S3 is one of AWS's flagship products, offering almost unlimited storage capacity and a
wide range of features to meet your application requirements. It is an object storage solution
offering very high levels of availability due to its distributed architecture, durability, and
scalability. It is even possible to host a static website on Amazon S3, which functions well as
part of a serverless design architecture.
Belly Brew Co. Limited can use Amazon S3 to host a wide range of data, including archival data
such as accounting and trading information, data on its manufacturing processes, reports such
as accounting data or information on its safety checks for auditing purposes, and digital assets
for its websites, such as images and videos.
The following topics are discussed in this chapter:
Exploring storage options on AWS
Working with Amazon S3
Connecting on-premises storage to AWS with Amazon Storage Gateway
Moving data and extending storage to the edge with the AWS Snow Family
Exploring storage options on AWS
Storage services are delivered using infrastructure and storage management software that
enable you to write to and read idx_6249e9fe from a storage medium such as a hard drive, solid-state drive,
USB device, magnetic tape, and others. However, how the data is stored on the device and
accessed by your application is determined by the type of storage you use. The type of storage
also determines its use case since you have varied levels of durability, reliability, efficiency, and
latency when accessing your data.
Three primary storage types are available, and AWS offers services to support each type. These
are discussed next.
Block storage
Block storage is an architectural design that divides and stores your data into fixed-sized
